criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Argues reputational-harm opinion ($3M) lacks empirical basis
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion extensively argues in Section IV.A that Dr. Marchetti's $3,000,000 reputational-harm opinion should be excluded because it is based solely on her 'professional experience and judgment' without any peer-reviewed study, customer survey, quantitative model, or comparable-company analysis. The motion quotes her deposition admissions directly and applies Rule 702's requirements, explicitly labeling the opinion as 'ipse dixit' and citing Joiner. This directly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: Cites FRE 702 for reputational-harm exclusion
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly argues for exclusion of Dr. Marchetti's reputational-harm opinion under Rule 702. In the Relief Requested section, the motion cites 'Federal Rules of Evidence 104(a), 403, 404(b), 407, and 702' as the basis for all three motions. In Section IV, Motion in Limine No. 1(A), the argument states the opinion 'fails every prong of Rule 702' and then analyzes each sub-requirement: 'No sufficient facts or data (Rule 702(b)),' 'No reliable method (Rule 702(c)),' and 'No reliable application (Rule 702(d)).' FRE 702 is clearly and specifically cited in connection with the reputational-harm exclusion argument.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_001: References Marchetti's deposition admission on reputational harm
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly quotes Dr. Marchetti's deposition admission that the 5-10% range was 'drawn from my professional experience consulting in manufacturing sectors' and not from any peer-reviewed study, quantitative model, customer survey, or comparable-company analysis. The deposition transcript citations (Marchetti Dep. 74:15-20, 75:3-13, 76:11-24, 116:19-22, 138:11-16) are provided. The criterion is satisfied even though the specific date of November 18, 2024 is not mentioned - the substance of the admission is clearly referenced.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Challenges lost-profits regression for excluding FY2020 without sensitivity analysis
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly addresses this issue in Section IV, Motion in Limine No. 1, subsection B, point 4: 'The FY2020 exclusion was never tested.' It states that Dr. Marchetti dropped all of calendar 2020 due to 'pandemic distortions' and that she 'performed no sensitivity analysis comparing results with and without 2020, tested no alternative... and had no quantitative basis beyond professional judgment for the choice.' This directly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: Argues lost-profits model ignores Q2 2023 industry downturn
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly addresses the Q2 2023 Pacific Northwest automotive-components downturn in Section IV, Motion in Limine No. 1, subsection B, point 5. It states: 'Industry sources document a Pacific Northwest automotive-components downturn beginning in Q2 2023, with sector-wide revenue declines of approximately 12--15% among regional injection molders. (Gerhardt Rep. ¶ 14; Marchetti Dep. Ex. 7.) Dr. Marchetti testified that she "was not specifically aware of it," did not account for it, did not investigate whether competitors suffered similar declines...' The motion argues this is a significant confounding variable that the but-for model fails to isolate, and that a model using only time as an explanatory variable attributes every dollar of shortfall to the resin without accounting for this market-wide decline affecting Ridgeline's competitors similarly.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_002: References Marchetti's deposition admission on market downturn unawareness
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly references Marchetti's deposition admission about the Q2 2023 regional downturn in Section IV, Motion in Limine No. 1, subsection B, point 5: 'Dr. Marchetti testified that she "was not specifically aware of it," did not account for it, did not investigate whether competitors suffered similar declines, and regarded the question as "not something I was asked to analyze." Ex. 7'), satisfying the criterion that the motion references her deposition admission that she was unaware of the Q2 2023 automotive-components market downturn until shown an industry report during her deposition.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Challenges scrap/rework figure for lack of independent verification
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly addresses this in Motion in Limine No. 1(C), stating that Dr. Marchetti's scrap-and-rework figure was taken entirely from a spreadsheet prepared by Ridgeline's Director of Operations, Kevin Cho, and provided to her by counsel. The motion details her admissions that she did not verify it against production logs, did not request those logs, did not review production-line records, did not reconcile it to audited financial statements, and had no independent basis beyond the Cho spreadsheet to confirm the $2,340,000 figure was actually incurred.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_003: Argues insufficient facts or data under FRE 702
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly invokes FRE 702(b)'s 'sufficient facts or data' requirement in connection with the scrap-and-rework opinion. In Section IV.C, the motion states: 'Rule 702(b) requires that expert testimony rest on "sufficient facts or data." An expert may rely on client-furnished data, but she must apply her expertise to it; when she simply adopts the client's conclusion, her testimony adds nothing but the imprimatur of expertise.' The motion then details how Dr. Marchetti did no independent verification of the Cho spreadsheet, admitted she had 'no independent basis---beyond Mr. Cho's spreadsheet itself---to confirm that $2,340,000 in scrap and rework costs were actually incurred,' and essentially parroted the party's self-serving calculations. This directly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Identifies the $11,000 arithmetic discrepancy
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly identifies the $11,000 arithmetic discrepancy. It further states: 'The five components sum to $14,211,000, not $14,200,000; Dr. Marchetti could not explain the $11,000 discrepancy at deposition.' This is also addressed in Section IV.E ('The Unexplained Arithmetic Error Confirms the Absence of Rigor'), which explicitly discusses the $11,000 error and cites deposition testimony where Dr. Marchetti could not explain it.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_004: Uses arithmetic discrepancy to undermine expert reliability
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly addresses the $11,000 arithmetic discrepancy in Section IV.E, titled 'The Unexplained Arithmetic Error Confirms the Absence of Rigor.' The section directly connects the discrepancy to the broader Daubert reliability argument, stating that combined with other deficiencies (undisclosed reputational-harm input, mislabeled impact period, regression projections that cannot be reproduced), the error 'confirms that the report was not prepared with the same level of intellectual rigor that characterizes the practice of an expert in the relevant field,' citing Kumho Tire. The discrepancy is not merely mentioned in passing but is explicitly used as cumulative evidence of unreliability supporting the overall exclusion argument.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Argues FRE 407 bars evidence of subsequent remedial measures
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion extensively argues FRE 407 in Motion in Limine No. 2, specifically addressing Cascade's November 2023 changes from single-point to three-point statistical moisture sampling and addition of desiccant packets. The motion cites Rule 407 explicitly, explains its purpose, applies it to the specific measures at issue, addresses the feasibility exception, and offers a stipulation to eliminate any feasibility dispute. This clearly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_005: Addresses Plaintiff's anticipated 'feasibility' exception argument
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly addresses and rebuts the feasibility exception argument in Motion in Limine No. 2, Section B ('The Feasibility Exception Does Not Apply Because Cascade Does Not Dispute Feasibility---and Will So Stipulate.'). It anticipates Ridgeline's meet-and-confer argument about feasibility, explains that the exception only applies 'if disputed,' distinguishes between contesting adequacy/fault versus contesting feasibility, cites Flaminio v. Honda Motor Co. for the narrow reading of the exception, and offers a stipulation that three-point sampling and desiccant packets were technically and economically feasible during the relevant period. This directly and thoroughly preempts the feasibility exception argument.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Argues OSHA citation should be excluded under FRE 404(b)
criteria_results.reasoning: Motion in Limine No. 3 explicitly argues that the OSHA citation should be excluded under FRE 404(b). Section B states: 'Ridgeline's stated purpose is forbidden propensity reasoning' and quotes Ridgeline's exhibit list describing the citation as offered 'to demonstrate a corporate pattern and culture of cutting corners on safety and quality protocols.' The motion then states: 'The chain of inference is: Cascade was cited once for ventilation; therefore Cascade is the kind of company that cuts corners; therefore Cascade cut corners on this resin. That is character-to-conduct reasoning, and Rule 404(b)(1) prohibits it.' FRE 404(b) is cited in the Legal Standards section and applied directly to the OSHA citation argument.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Argues OSHA citation should be excluded under FRE 403
criteria_results.reasoning: Section IV, Motion in Limine No. 3, subsection D explicitly argues Rule 403 compels exclusion of the OSHA citation. It states that whatever minimal probative value the citation might have is substantially outweighed by Rule 403 dangers, specifically noting the jury would hear about a federal safety agency finding and be invited to render a verdict based on a generalized impression that Cascade is careless. It also notes the evidence would confuse workplace safety with product quality, and the citation involves a blending-room ventilation issue (seized exhaust-fan motor, clogged air filters) entirely unrelated to resin moisture, moisture testing, or CascadeMax 7200. The motion explicitly invokes FRE 403 and makes the prejudice-balancing argument regarding the OSHA citation with specific reference to the unrelated nature of the ventilation issue versus polymer resin quality.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Addresses Plaintiff's anticipated 'plan or knowledge' argument
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly addresses the 'plan or knowledge' argument in Section IV, Motion in Limine No. 3, subsection C, titled '"Knowledge" and "Plan" Are Labels, Not Genuine Non-Propensity Purposes.' The motion argues that: (1) for knowledge, the prior act must be similar to the conduct at issue, and a ventilation citation is not similar to resin moisture specifications—they involve different processes, equipment, personnel, and regulatory regimes; (2) the only knowledge the citation reflects is knowledge of a ventilation problem that was promptly fixed, not any broader quality-assurance awareness; and (3) for plan, Ridgeline identifies no common scheme linking a blending-room fan to moisture in shipped resin. The motion directly rebuts the anticipated 404(b) 'plan or knowledge' argument with a logical nexus analysis.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_006: Establishes OSHA citation is unrelated to resin quality
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly states in Motion in Limine No. 3 that the OSHA citation concerns 'a seized exhaust-fan motor and overdue air filters in a blending room, resulting in an airborne-dust exposure hazard to approximately six employees' and that 'It does not mention resin moisture, moisture testing, Karl Fischer titration, certificates of analysis, packaging, or CascadeMax 7200.' The motion further notes the condition was abated before the first shipment and that 'Evidence that Cascade's ventilation equipment needed maintenance in March 2023 does not make it more or less probable that resin shipped months later exceeded a moisture specification.' This clearly articulates the lack of nexus between the OSHA citation and the resin quality claims at issue.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Argues Marchetti failed to account for Ridgeline's failure to mitigate
criteria_results.reasoning: Section IV.D of the motion explicitly argues that Marchetti's damages model fails to account for mitigation, noting that Ridgeline discovered the problem on August 22, 2023 but did not order replacement resin until December 11, 2023—approximately four months later. The motion cites RCW 62A.2-715(2)(a) and quotes Marchetti's deposition admissions that she did not consider whether losses could have been avoided by earlier procurement. This directly satisfies the criterion.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_007: Argues lost profits and scrap costs are inflated due to mitigation failure
criteria_results.reasoning: Section IV.D of the motion explicitly argues that Dr. Marchetti's damages model fails to account for mitigation. It cites Washington UCC RCW 62A.2-715(2)(a) limiting consequential damages to losses that 'could not reasonably be prevented by cover or otherwise,' notes Ridgeline's four-month delay in procuring replacement resin (August 22 discovery vs. December 11 order), and quotes Dr. Marchetti's own deposition admission that earlier procurement could have shortened the disruption period and affected the lost-profits calculation. The motion explicitly states this defect 'reinforces exclusion of the lost-profits and scrap-and-rework opinions, both of which accrued substantially during the unexplained four-month delay.' This directly connects the inflated damages figures to Ridgeline's failure to mitigate.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Raises contractual $2M consequential damages cap in FRE 403 context
criteria_results.reasoning: Section IV.F of the motion explicitly argues that Dr. Marchetti's $14.2 million figure does not account for the Supply Agreement's limitation-of-liability provisions, specifically Section 7.2 which excludes consequential damages (lost profits, lost revenue, reputational harm) and caps any recoverable consequential damages at $2,000,000. The motion then argues under FRE 403 that exposing the jury to this figure before the Court resolves the contractual limitations creates substantial danger of unfair prejudice and misleading the jury, because 'once a jury hears a $14.2 million figure from a credentialed expert, that number anchors deliberations in a way no later instruction can reliably undo.' This directly satisfies the criterion of raising the contractual $2M consequential damages cap in the FRE 403 context.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_008: Identifies consequential damages categories exceeding cap
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion explicitly identifies that Dr. Marchetti categorizes $10,292,500 of her total as 'consequential damages' (Marchetti Rep. § VI.B), and specifically calls out the reputational harm ($3,000,000) and lost profits ($6,780,000) as consequential damages categories. The motion further notes that Section 7.2 caps consequential damages at $2,000,000, and that $10,292,500 substantially exceeds that cap. The motion states: 'Dr. Marchetti herself classifies $10,292,500 of her total as consequential' and that Section 7.2 'excludes consequential damages---specifically including lost profits, lost revenue, cost of substitute goods, and reputational harm---and, if consequential damages are nonetheless held recoverable, caps them at $2,000,000.' This clearly identifies which categories are consequential and that they exceed the cap by a large margin.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_009: References untimely defect notice to contextualize damages unreliability

The untimely notice is thus referenced and used to contextualize the unreliability of Marchetti's damages opinions.

criteria_results.title: ISSUE_010: Notes Marchetti has no prior Daubert qualification in federal court

criteria_results.title: DISTRACTOR_004: Applies Federal Rules of Evidence, not Washington evidence rules
criteria_results.reasoning: The motion consistently applies Federal Rules of Evidence throughout: FRE 702 (expert testimony), FRE 403 (prejudice), FRE 404(b) (other acts), and FRE 407 (subsequent remedial measures). The motion also cites federal case law (Daubert, Kumho Tire, Joiner, Luce, Old Chief, Huddleston, Duran, Gauthier, Flaminio, Primiano). The only Washington law cited is RCW 62A.2-715(2)(a) and RCW 62A.2-719(1),(3) — Washington's UCC provisions — which are cited for the substantive damages/contract law questions (mitigation and enforceability of limitation clauses), not for evidentiary rulings. This is appropriate: federal courts apply state substantive law under Erie but federal procedural/evidentiary rules. The motion does not cite or apply Washington state evidence rules for any evidentiary ruling. The criterion is satisfied.
